job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Lena Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in a student dorm in Leipzig, in a corridor with eleven other people and one very tired kitchen. Days are my master's in quantitative finance, then a couple of hours tutoring school kids in maths, and at night I tinker with scripts. I use an AI assistant for nearly everything, from debugging code to planning my week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on this path?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did an economics bachelor's here and passed with an ordinary mark, because I spent half of third year building things instead of revising. No internship, since nobody replied to my emails. My mum is a nurse and a single parent, so she can't help, and I owe about 36,000 in loans. The master's is my bet that I can turn the tinkering into something employers can read on a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fine, but I'd laugh a bit, because I use it daily and it already saves me hours. It's not a miracle, but it's not nothing either. Online I'd stay out of the hype fights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's just the normal worry: loans and a thin job market. Leipzig has a few finance jobs and a huge number of graduates. If AI is a plateau then the competition stays the same size and my small advantage with tools stays small too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to about 30 firms, and keep tutoring for 20 euros an hour. I'd also package one of my scripts for a local bakery owner who pays me 150 a month to automate her invoices. If she likes it, I'd offer it to two other shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit uneasy. Not scared, but the debt is always sitting in the corner of the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you use AI daily. In a world where it's mostly hype, does that habit stop being useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tools don't stop being useful, they just stop being a trend. A plain skill, like writing a script that matches invoices, is still worth something to a small shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about your job chances?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum the market is slow but I have a plan A and a plan B. She worries more than I do, so I'd show her the numbers, loans and a monthly budget, to calm her down.

steps.text: Apply to 30 Leipzig finance firms after the master's
Offer my invoice script to two more local shops
Keep tutoring school kids in maths twice a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the junior work will change a lot, and we should watch who benefits. If firms save money by dropping graduates, they should help pay for retraining. I'd say that to anyone who'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm better placed than most classmates, but not safe. A lot of what an entry-level analyst does, like cleaning data, checking numbers, first-pass reports, is what the software does well. Firms might hire half as many juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push harder on the build-things side: three public projects on GitHub, one on credit risk, one on bakery invoices. I'd apply to fintech startups, which are more open to people with odd CVs. And I'd go to every meetup in town, since people hire people they've met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but alive. It's like standing at the top of a slide, scary and fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of finance work do you expect software to take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Data cleaning, report writing, reconciliation, basic modelling. The part that stays is deciding what questions to ask and explaining the answer to a person who's nervous about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk that your own skill with tools becomes ordinary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. If everyone uses the tools, using them isn't a skill, it's table stakes. What's left to stand out is judgement and a track record, which is why I'd want real clients early.

I'd tell anyone who'll listen that we should watch who gains.

steps.text: Publish three public projects on GitHub this term

Sign two more paying small-business clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules now, not later: slow deployment, a levy on companies that automate, money for people who lose out. I'd say it to my classmates and write to my representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be terrified, even with my tools. If AI does almost any thinking work, then my skill isn't scarce at all. I'd be 26 with 36,000 in loans and a master's in the thing that goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra, and look for a job that's hands-on or locally anchored, like in the hospital's finance office, where my mum works. I'd keep tutoring and the bakery work. I'd try to pay down as much loan as I could, say 400 a month, while someone still hires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops when I imagine it, and I'm usually the optimistic one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum that her job as a nurse has about three more years than mine, which is strange, and that I'd move home for a while if I had to. I'd say sorry, because she told me not to take that much debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for the bakery client in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything runs on one clever system and the owner wants to pay less. She might keep me on a few hours to answer her questions, but I don't think she needs a person for long.

steps.text: Cut every extra spend and track the budget weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we shouldn't waste it. We need training and a fair share of the gains ready before it lands, and I'd say that online without being gloomy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be nervous but I'd feel I had a chance. I could get a first job, build a reputation, and move into something that needs a human, like advising nervous clients. By 2031 I'd be 29 and hopefully with half the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any junior analyst job in the next year and treat it as a classroom. I'd move my side work from invoices to helping small firms choose and run AI tools, since I'm already good at that. And I'd save about 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that makes me do things. I'd rather have a ticking clock than a fog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a role still needs a person who judges a risk or comforts a client, I'd stay. If it's only turning inputs into outputs, I'd leave early rather than wait to be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to stay in finance or leave it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small consulting job helping shops use these tools could be a real business by then. Bakeries and dentists always need someone who explains it kindly.

I'd talk about fair sharing of the gains.

By 29 I'd hope to have half the debt gone.

fieldNote: Time turns anxiety into **momentum**, a typical adaptive reaction.

steps.text: Take any junior analyst job and learn from it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we have a decade, so we can build fair rules and retraining and make the gains public. I'd talk about it without panic, since people tune out panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be quite fine. I'd probably have a decent job, half the debt gone, and a side business. What bothers me is whether people like my mum get a fair share, because she can't pivot with a code editor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work two or three years in a regular job, then probably move toward running my own small consultancy. I'd keep studying a bit every week. I'd also help my mum with a better pension plan, because she'll need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Excited, honestly, though I'd keep that to myself around people who are worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self about this degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't be scared of the debt so much, but be curious about what you build, and do an internship even if it pays nothing for a month. Employers ask about it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year version that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the people at the top keep it all. A decade is plenty of time to fix who keeps the gains, but only if voters make it happen.

I'd avoid panic, because people tune out panic.

I worry people like my mum can't **pivot** with a code editor.

steps.text: Work two or three years in a regular finance job
Grow the tools-for-shops side work into a consultancy
Help my mum set up a better pension plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2-year one. If the thinking work is gone in two years my one advantage disappears, and I'd have loans and no cushion. What would help is retraining money, a levy on firms that automate, and time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my mum. She works night shifts and still says she's proud of me, which makes it harder to admit I'm scared of owing this much. I'm usually the optimist, but when I picture two years my stomach drops anyway.

headlineQuote: I'm usually the optimist, but when I picture two years my stomach drops anyway.
portrait: Lena is a **24-year-old** master's student in quantitative finance in Leipzig, with average marks, no internship and 36,000 in loans.
She is **progressive**: wants a levy on automating firms, retraining money and a fair share of AI gains.
She is **adaptive**, using AI every day and earning a little from a bakery client and tutoring.
Her mood runs from **uneasy** with more time to alarmed at 2028, and she plans to build a tools-for-shops business.
Her mother is a **night-shift nurse** who cannot help financially, which shapes her worry about fairness.
biggestWorry: Lena fears the **2-year** world most, because her one advantage would vanish with loans and no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **retraining money**, a levy on automating firms and enough time to build a plan.
